## Cardiovascular Outcome Registries and Research (CORR)

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
### 1997 CORR

-   SAS shop
-   Goal: any analyst can pick up any job
-   Folder structure with file naming conventions
-   A social contract — loosely enforced
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Today

-   R and SAS hybrid
-   Team grows to 19 (and more)
-   Conventions extended to R
:::
:::::

SAS/C PROC `hazard` for survival analysis (1986).

R package `randomForestSRC` survival, regression, classification (2007).

R package `ggRandomForests` RFSRC graphics (2012).

[Discipline doesn't scale under production pressure]{style="color: #006B5E; font-weight: bold;"}


::: notes
I work in Cardiovascular Outcomes Registries and Research, we're part of the Heart, Vascular and thoracic Institute at the Cleveland Clinic. CORR was started in 1997, with the arrival of our director Dr. Eugene Blackstone. We started as a pure SAS, with a small team. We had a goal of being able to hand off a study easily as required. These handoffs required using a social contract held by discipline within the team. Over time, R entered by evolution. The goal is to use the best methodology to answer the scientific questions.

Our primary in house methods started with PROC hazard, a SAS/C method. In 2007, Dr. Ishwaran developed randomForestSRC in CORR, and I wrote ggRandomForests to simplify plotting the forest outputs.

As we've grown, we're seeing that discipline alone doesn't scale easily.

:::

::: notes
We are concerned with the scale that this social contract has to support. 19 staff driving 150 data requests delivered directly to researchers. Additionally, we produce about 100+ presentations, and 50 manuscripts a year — all feeding into last years 1,100 HVTI publications. Every inefficiency in our system multiplies across that. This talk is directly addressing what "operating at scale" means. 
:::

::: notes
Corr includes 19 data staff split between disciplines three disciplines. Data Engineers focus primarily on getting data from medical systems into our data warehouse, primarily using python. Stat programmers assemble analysis data sets primarily in SAS. Biostatisticans build an analysis report using SAS and R. Our researcher collaborators convert the analysis report into manuscripts and presentations. Data flows through systems; people transform it at each step. The biostatistician sits at the core — taking analysis dataset and producing an Analysis Report that researchers can use to construct a manuscript. Since this conference is an audience of R users, we can focus on the Biostats component of the pipeline.
:::

Biostats run **jobs**, write **an Analysis Report**.

Researchers write the manuscript.

::: notes
The main deliverable of the team is the Analysis Report. SAS and R jobs are implementation detail — what our audience cares about is the report that comes out the other side. Researchers bring the questions, formed as hypothesis. This drives the process. What data is required to answer these questions? CORR determines the statistical approaches, in collaboration with researchers refining the questions. Figures and tables communicate the results to the end audience.

Scaling the team means making every step of that pipeline reliable and handoff-ready. We still maintain the goal of "any analyst can pick up any job", we call it "bus insurance". Can another analyst step in and pick up where ever you are, and continue the work.

:::

## Reproducibility at scale — Three Focus Areas {background-color="#006B5E"}

::: {style="font-size: 1.8em; line-height: 1.8;"}
1. Data ingestion
2. Model building
3. Figures and tables
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.5em; margin-top: 1em; font-style: italic; opacity: 0.85;"}
Make the safe path the easy path.
:::

::: notes
These are the three places where reproducibility breaks down in practice. Each section follows the same structure: here's the failure mode, here's what we're doing about it.

Make the safe path the easy path. We already do a lot of mental work to compensate for the gaps — remembering which dataset is current, keeping track of which version of a function ran, manually assembling figures into a report. The goal isn't to add process on top of that — it's to replace that mental overhead with automation. Checksums instead of memory. Package versions instead of tribal knowledge. Quarto instead of copy-paste.

Long term, the vision is an audit process that runs automatically — not a checklist someone fills out, but a system that tells you whether the analysis is reproducible before you have to ask. We're not there yet, but every piece we put in place moves us closer.
:::

::: notes
The folder structure isn't the problem — it works. Dataset filenaming MIGHT work. We've all seen these naming "strategies". We also used file system "modified dates" implicitly, but those are fragile and change in uncontrolled ways.

We want to standardize our data with a simple, automatic approach...  Start by making the file date part of the standard. Adding the date to the filename when the file is created, whcih won't change if the file is moved. 

That doesn't solve the whole problem, we still need to track what happens inside the file. What if the file gets overwritten when a data extract gets updated? Naming and modified dates weren't designed for this job.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 1.4em; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
*Is this the right data? Has it changed?*
:::

## How we're addressing it [In development]{.badge-dev}

**Layer governance on top of existing structure.**

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
### What we have

::: {style="font-size: 1.7em;"}
```
study_root/
  analyses/      ← jobs
  datasets/      ← *this problem*
  descriptive/
  distributions/
  documents/     ← deliverables
  estimates/     ← cached results
  graphs/        ← pdf
```
:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### What we're adding

-   Date in the filename<br>[never overwrite]{.muted}
-   Dataset manifest<br>[source, date, parameters]{.muted}
-   Checksum<br>[detect silent changes]{.muted}
-   Audit trail<br>[job ↔ manifest]{.muted}
:::
:::::

::: notes
The folder structure is already there and it works. Jobs under analysis read datasets and write models and results to estimates, and generate graphs. Documents contain deliverables. Inside datasets/ — filenames contain the date they were written, programatically. 

A dataset Manifest is created with a checksum registration before we first USE a data file. This must be separate from the dataset creation and done before we build the individual analysis jobs. 

We are building a data audit trail, checked inside the analysis jobs. Importantly, this CAN be done regardless of the analysis platform.
:::

## Manifest + checksum in practice [In development]{.badge-dev}

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
**`datasets/built260430.manifest.yml`**

```yaml
dataset:      built260430.sas7bdat
source:       Cardiopulse / STS registry v2.1
pulled_by:    data_manager
pull_date:    2026-04-30
sha256:       a3f8c2d1e4b7f093...
observations: 12847
variables:    428
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
**Register explicitly — separate from build**

```r
digest::digest(
  "datasets/built260430.sas7bdat",
  algo = "sha256", file = TRUE)
```

**Verify before analysis**

```r
stored  <- yaml::read_yaml(
  "datasets/built260430.manifest.yml")$sha256
current <- digest::digest(
  "datasets/built260430.sas7bdat",
  algo = "sha256", file = TRUE)
stopifnot(current == stored)
```

[Filename says *when*. Checksum says *whether*.]{.muted}
:::

:::::

::: notes
The checksum is stored in the manifest at registration. This is deliberately separate from file creation. If the file is overwritten accidently (extract re-run, data corrected), the old checksum stays in the manifest and jobs will fail until someone consciously re-registers. The social contract now is `never over write a dated dataset."

This makes rebuilds fail loudly by default. The date-stamped filename tells you when the extract was pulled; the checksum tells you whether the file you're reading now is the same one that was registered. 

It doesn't tell you a new dataset file exists — it only indicates that the registered one hasn't changed.
:::

. . .

Rebuild without re-registering → every downstream job fails.
<br>
**That failure is the feature.**

# Model Building {background-color="#34495e"}

Make the safe path the easy path.

## Problem: R and SAS Environments

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**SAS**

-   SAS version not locked to a study
-   Shared Macro library unversioned
-   Shared server
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**R & RStudio**

-   R version is not locked to a study
-   Shared Package library — package versions drift
-   Shared server 
-   Serialized models in `estimates/` **fail to load**
-   Results don't match — or the job won't run
:::
:::::

::: notes
In model building, we have a few problems to address. First, regardless of the platform, SAS and R versions are not locked into the study. We work on a shared disk, with Rstudio server and a shared SAS instance. Neither platform captures the environment. SAS's shared server setup makes it invisible; RStudio can help with Projects, if we use them. The way R uses a global package library makes package versions fragile. The failure modes look different but the root cause is the same: no one pinned the environment to the study.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 1.4em; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
*Can you reproduce this analysis six months from now?*
:::

## R: `renv` with RStudio projects [In flight]{.badge-inflight}

```{=html}
<style>
.renv-split { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 44px 1fr; gap: 0; }
.renv-bad { background: #fdf2f2; border: 2px solid #e74c3c; border-radius: 8px 0 0 8px; padding: 12px 16px; display: flex; flex-direction: column; }
.renv-good { background: #f0faf5; border: 2px solid #006B5E; border-radius: 0 8px 8px 0; padding: 12px 16px; display: flex; flex-direction: column; }
.renv-arr { display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; font-size: 1.8em; color: #aaa; background: #f4f4f4; }
.renv-head { font-size: 0.78em; font-weight: 700; margin-bottom: 8px; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: 0.05em; padding-bottom: 5px; border-bottom: 2px solid currentColor; }
.renv-bad .renv-head { color: #c0392b; }
.renv-good .renv-head { color: #006B5E; }
.renv-item { font-size: 0.72em; padding: 4px 0; border-bottom: 1px solid rgba(0,0,0,0.07); line-height: 1.4; color: #333; }
.renv-step { font-size: 0.74em; font-weight: 700; color: #006B5E; margin-top: 7px; margin-bottom: 2px; }
.renv-step-sub { font-size: 0.62em; color: #888; margin-bottom: 3px; }
.renv-code { background: #1e1e1e; color: #ccc; border-radius: 4px; padding: 6px 10px; font-family: 'Courier New', monospace; font-size: 0.6em; line-height: 1.7; }
.renv-lock { background: #006B5E; color: #fff; border-radius: 6px; padding: 5px 10px; text-align: center; font-size: 0.6em; font-weight: 700; line-height: 1.6; margin: 5px auto; display: block; width: fit-content; }
.renv-ok { font-size: 0.74em; color: #006B5E; font-weight: 600; margin-top: 5px; line-height: 1.5; }
</style>

<div class="renv-split">
  <div class="renv-bad">
    <div class="renv-head">Without renv</div>
    <div class="renv-item">Packages installed globally &mdash; shared across all projects</div>
    <div class="renv-item"><code>update.packages()</code> breaks other analyses silently</div>
    <div class="renv-item">Serialized models in <code>estimates/</code> fail to load 6 months later</div>
    <div class="renv-item">&ldquo;Works on my machine&rdquo; &mdash; but not yours</div>
    <div class="renv-item">New analyst hunts down exact versions to reproduce results</div>
  </div>
  <div class="renv-arr">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="renv-good">
    <div class="renv-head">With renv</div>
    <div class="renv-step">Day 1 &mdash; any analyst, any machine</div>
    <div class="renv-step-sub">Isolate the project library and freeze it</div>
    <div class="renv-code">
      <span style="color:#569cd6;">renv</span>::init()&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<span style="color:#6a9955;"># isolate library</span><br>
      <span style="color:#569cd6;">renv</span>::install(<span style="color:#ce9178;">"ehrlinger/hvtiPlotR"</span>)<br>
      <span style="color:#569cd6;">renv</span>::snapshot()&nbsp;&nbsp;<span style="color:#6a9955;"># freeze versions</span>
    </div>
    <div class="renv-lock">renv.lock &mdash; R 4.4.1 &middot; hvtiPlotR 0.3.2 &middot; &hellip;<br><span style="font-weight:400;">commit this; it travels with the project</span></div>
    <div class="renv-step">6 months later &mdash; different analyst, different machine</div>
    <div class="renv-step-sub">Open .Rproj, run one command</div>
    <div class="renv-code">
      <span style="color:#569cd6;">renv</span>::restore()&nbsp;&nbsp;<span style="color:#6a9955;"># rebuilds library from renv.lock</span>
    </div>
    <div class="renv-ok">Same packages. Same results. The job belongs to the team.</div>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: notes
The key word is "handoff." Python has virtual environments, R' has the `renv` package track the environment.

On day 1, we initialize `renv` and take a snapshot of the package library and R version. This makes the jobs transferable, not just reproducible on your own machine. The lockfile travels with the project; the library itself gets rebuilt locally on renv::restore(). 

SAS has no equivalent — it is less volatile than R, but environments are still an open problem.
:::

## Problem: Shared function libraries aren't versioned

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**SAS macro library**

-   Centralized — everyone calls the same macros
-   Not versioned — no record of which version ran
-   Changes propagate silently
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**R functions**

-   Copied at study creation — diverges immediately
-   Fixes stay local; no propagation
-   In-flight studies never get updates
:::
:::::

::: notes
Our strategy for SAS and R shared functions surface two different failure modes, both equally bad. 

SAS has a centralized macro library, but we don't control when changes land — every study gets every update whether ready or not. 

R functions are typically copied into a study at creation. This isolates studies from each other but also from function improvements or fixes stay local and often diverge over time.

Neither platform has a deliberate, versioned release process.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 1.4em; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
*SAS: did that update break something? R: did anyone else get that fix?*
:::

## R: internal packages (SAS macros) [In development]{.badge-dev}

An R package **is** a versioned, distributable library.

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Functions in the study folder**

- Frozen at copy
- Fixes don't propagate
- No version record
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Code in a package**

- One canonical version
- Pull fixes deliberately with `renv::update()`
- Examples travel with code, double as tests
:::
:::::

::: notes
Packages are better than scattered copies, but the governance problems shift rather than disappear. combined with `renv`, the version choice becomes explicit and deliberate — which is exactly the point.
:::

. . .

**The hard problems shift — they don't disappear.**

- Someone must own releases.
- Communication of improvements to the teams
- Studies must change versions deliberately. **controlled**

## Problem: Code and results live separately

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**SAS — partially solved this**

-   `.lst` pairs code and output
-   Figures still separate files

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**R scripts — no equivalent**

-   Code and output in separate files
-   No standard structure
-   Figures disconnected from code
:::
:::::

::: notes
Code and results are note connected. This problem transends the platform again. Jupyter. notebooks, SAS and R all have interactive modes. In SAS we solved this by "mandating" you run the whole job before leaving the job (every night? maybe...). The .lst file is the output. You'd do the same with jupyter notebooks... R scripts have no equivalent yet. 
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 1.4em; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
*Can a new analyst navigate this job without asking whoever wrote it?*
:::

## Quarto templates [In development]{.badge-dev}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**`report.qmd` = `job.sas`**

-   Code and output in one document
-   Figures inline
-   Renders to HTML, PDF, Word

**Always render before committing.**
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Standard 4-section template**

```markdown
# Data.qmd
Ingestion, exclusions, cohort description

# Methods.qmd
Model specification and assumptions

# Explainability.qmd
Diagnostics, sensitivity checks

# Results.qmd
Tables, figures, interpretation
```

[The structure is the contract.]{.muted}
:::
:::::

::: notes
Quarto is analogous to the sas job and lst files. A single unified report that includes R code and the output. The report has the advantage of including real figures inline. And renders to a deliverable report, in html, pdf or even word.

The pitch to SAS analysts isn't just "learn this new tool" (I tried that) — it's "get what you already have in .lst, but with real figures inline and a structure everyone agrees on." 

We're working on a 4-section template structure as the standard: Short enough chunks to be understandable, consistent enough to navigate, flexible enough to cover every study type. We may be able to connect the steps using a `bookdown` approacj.

There is still an underlying copy/paste problem — both SAS jobs and R scripts are copied from a central templates folder, meaning in-flight studies don't implicitly get updates. Quarto and R packages are the foundation we're building first before tackling that propagation problem.
:::

Make the safe path the easy path.

## The Problem: Publication-quality graphics

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**SAS: `plot.sas`**

- Hard-won publication quality
- Each output target: more manual effort

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**R: `ggplot2`**

- Same per-target effort problem
- No shared themes or palettes
:::
:::::

::: notes
We spent an extraordinary amount of effort to make SAS graph behave with our plot.sas macro. we bent SAS graphics into publication quality for manuscripts, but we never solved the presentation problem. Methods we used to use broke, so every presentation now requires a lot of manual work.

ggplot2 is more flexible but customizing the output for manuscript and presentations still requires quite a bit of effort. 
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 1.4em; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
*Can we capture that effort once — make figures consistent?*
:::

## R: standardized pipeline [In flight]{.badge-inflight}

**The package does the hard work. The analyst decorates.**

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Package owns**

- The statistical transform
- The base figure — correct by construction
- Themes: manuscript, PowerPoint, poster

**Analyst owns**

- Axis labels, annotations
- Nothing else needs to change
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
# Package handles the figure
fig <- plot(corr_analysis(data))

# Analyst decorates to context
fig +
  hv_theme("manuscript") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  annotate("text", ...)
```

*If it looks like the package example, it's correct.*
:::
:::::

::: notes
Our internal hvtiPlotR package addresses this — capturing the effort in a package and enforcing shared standards through an S3 pattern. The S3 pattern matters because it separates concerns cleanly. The transform function does the statistical work and returns a typed object. The plot method knows how to visualize that object and returns a ggplot object. The analyst's job is decoration — choosing scales, adding annotations — not rebuilding the figure from scratch. hvtiPlotR::themes diverge between the target manuscript or presentations formatting.

The package examples are the documentation AND the quality standard: if your figure matches the example, it's correct. This is how we recover and improve consistency in how we deliver publication quality figures from R.
:::

## Our visualization packages [In flight]{.badge-inflight}

**`ggRandomForests`** — [github.com/ehrlinger/ggRandomForests](https://github.com/ehrlinger/ggRandomForests)

Variable importance, partial depth, minimal depth — `ggplot2` for `randomForestSRC`.

<br>

**`hvtiPlotR`** — [github.com/ehrlinger/hvtiPlotR](https://github.com/ehrlinger/hvtiPlotR)

Survival curves, hazard plots, forest plots in CORR themes. 

Bridges `ggplot2` to `plot.sas` standards.

<br>

*As the science keeps moving and CORR eveolves, so do the packages.*

::: notes
ggRandomForests was the proof of concept — born from an internal need, built as a package, and eventually adopted externally. It was removed from CRAN because of dependency drift, not design failure; the pattern still holds. hvtiPlotR applies the same model to CORR-specific plot types.

These packages are always in development — the science keeps moving, and the package has to keep up. That's a governance problem as much as a technical one.
:::

## The framing shift that mattered {background-color="#34495e"}

::: {style="font-size: 1.8em; line-height: 1.5; margin-bottom: 0.8em;"}
"Reproducibility" → **"Production reliability"**
:::

*"Any biostatistician can pick up any job."*

The tools don't change. The reason to adopt them does.

::: notes
To wrap up, I've been working on these pain points in CORR for a long time. The Reproducibility framing failed — it reads as an academic virtue, something you do for reviewers when asked. The Production reliability framing lands differently with the team: it's about whether someone else can pick up your job on a Monday morning when you're out sick. Same tools, same practices — but the reason to adopt them shifts from "good science hygiene" to "your teammates won't be stranded." The second framing can help with buy-in. 

Make the right path the easy path means the standards have to be lower-friction than the workaround, or people will always take the workaround. Being transparent, it's still takes work for people to change their ways... even if the path is "hypothetically easier", roll out is still a learning experience and being done under production pressure.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 1.5em; margin-top: 0.5em; font-style: italic;"}
Make the safe path the easy path.
:::
